task.description:
CODE-DESIGNER pass (WF-02 Step 1) for REQ-168 (queue task 320, GH#620). Read REQ-168's full entry in docs/requirements.yaml (id: REQ-168) before anything else -- read it in full, do not work from this summary alone. Produce a design artefact under lib/letflow/design/ (e.g. req168-wasm-memory-isolation.md) per this project's CODE-DESIGNER conventions, design-only (zero implementation code -- @spec/@type/interface-level content only). This is the single highest-stakes WASM design so far: its own acceptance criterion's failure mode is a HOST CRASH, which under this project's chosen runtime (wasmex/Wasmtime via NIF, decision 0014) means the BEAM NODE itself, not a request or even a single process. Treat verification accordingly -- every claim about what makes a wasmex memory read/write operation safe vs. unsafe MUST be independently, live-verified against the real installed dependency (this pipeline's last three WASM designs each required a rework round after this exact kind of unverified claim was caught by CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR; this one has the least room for error of any of them, since a wrong claim here risks a real node crash if ELIXIR-DEV or a later requirement trusts it).

Core substance: WASM-08 requires a SINGLE validation function that every host-side read of guest linear memory goes through, bounds-checking a (offset, length) pair against the instance's REAL current memory size before any dereference -- rejecting (a) an offset beyond memory size, (b) a length that would run past the memory end, and (c) an offset+length pair that integer-overflows (wraps around, which on a naive `offset + length <= size` check without overflow protection could pass a malicious pair that wraps past the max integer boundary and appears in-range). A malformed pair must yield a structured error/trap that the caller can pattern-match on, never an exception/exit propagating out of the validation function and never (this is the actual point of the requirement) a native-level fault that takes down the BEAM node. The design must also cover per-instance memory isolation: prove two separate instances of the same module do not share linear memory (a write in one is never observable via a read in the other) -- verify this live, don't assume it from Wasmtime's general architecture.

MANDATORY LIVE VERIFICATION (read deps/wasmex/lib/wasmex/memory.ex directly first -- it has size/2, grow/2, get_byte/3, set_byte/4, write_binary/4, read_binary/4, read_string/4): (1) verify live what Wasmex.Memory.size/2 actually returns (pages? bytes? both?) and how to derive the real byte-length boundary from it; (2) verify live what happens when you call Wasmex.Memory.read_binary/4 (or get_byte/3) with an offset/length that is genuinely out of bounds against a real instance's real memory -- does it return a clean {:error, _}, does it raise, does it crash the calling process, or (worst case) does it crash the BEAM node itself -- this is the single most safety-critical empirical fact this design depends on, so verify it with an actual out-of-bounds read against a real Wasmex memory handle, not by reading NIF source comments; (3) verify live whether wasmex/Wasmtime's own NIF-level implementation already performs bounds-checking BEFORE your Elixir-level validation function would ever run (if wasmex's read_binary/4 already safely rejects out-of-bounds reads with a clean error tuple/exception rather than a native fault, that changes what your validation function's job actually is -- it may need to exist for the STRUCTURED-error-shape and overflow-arithmetic-safety guarantees WASM-08 asks for, even if the underlying NIF call turns out to already be crash-safe; if it does NOT already reject cleanly, your Elixir-level validation function is the ONLY thing standing between a malicious guest and a node crash, which must be stated explicitly and verified as your design's central safety claim); (4) verify live whether writing (Wasmex.Memory.write_binary/4 or set_byte/4) with an out-of-bounds offset/length has the same behavior as reading, or different; (5) verify live that two separate Wasmex.start_link/1-produced instances of the identical module bytes have genuinely independent memory (write a value via one instance's Wasmex.Memory handle, read the same address via the other instance's handle, confirm no leak).

Decide where this validation function lives -- likely a new module (e.g. Letflow.Engine.Wasm.MemoryGuard or similar) rather than folding into ModuleRegistry/CapabilityGate, since this is a distinct concern (runtime pointer validation on every host-function call, not registration-time or instantiation-time) -- follow this project's established separation-of-concerns precedent (req155 sec4.4, already cited by req166/req167). Since REQ-171/172 (host API) don't exist yet, this design's tests will need to exercise the validation function directly against a real Wasmex.Memory handle from a test-fixture instance, not through a real host function call (there isn't one yet) -- state this explicitly as the design's test strategy, mirroring how req167's registry used placeholder host functions.

The moduledoc must state honestly (per the requirement's own scope note 4): this validation prevents the HOST from dereferencing a bad pointer it read from Elixir-side memory-access calls; it does NOT bound a fault occurring inside Wasmtime's own native code/runtime itself, which remains the disclosed uncovered class per REQ-165's own moduledoc (cite it directly).
acceptance_criteria: AC1: a single validation function exists that every host-side read of guest memory goes through, and a repo search over lib/ restricted to '*.ex' shows no other guest-memory read path -- design must specify this function's exact signature and where callers (a currently-nonexistent host-function layer, per REQ-171/172) are expected to call it, plus how the design's own tests exercise it directly given no real host function exists yet.

AC2: a malformed pointer from a guest yields a structured error outcome to the caller and the BEAM node stays up -- design must state exactly what the live verification (per the methodology note above) found about wasmex's own out-of-bounds behavior, and specify the validation function's exact error shape and how it guarantees no exception/exit/native fault escapes.

AC3: tests cover at minimum an offset beyond memory size, a length running past the memory end, and an offset+length pair that overflows -- design must specify the exact bounds-check arithmetic (in words/pseudocode, no Elixir code) that correctly handles all three, particularly the overflow case (why a naive offset+length<=size check is unsafe, and what the design does instead).

AC4: two instances of the same module do not share linear memory -- design must specify how this is tested (write via one instance's Wasmex.Memory handle, read via the other's) and state the live-verification finding.

AC5: the moduledoc states this validation bounds host-side dereferences only, not a fault inside Wasmtime's own native code, mirroring REQ-165's disclosed residual class -- design must cite REQ-165's design doc's exact section making this disclosure.
AC6: mix test and mix compile --warnings-as-errors both pass -- not a design element, but the design's chosen types/signatures must give ELIXIR-DEV something both commands can meaningfully enforce.
Zero literal Elixir code in the design doc -- @spec/@type/interface descriptions only.
Full traceability table mapping every one of REQ-168's real acceptance criteria (read from docs/requirements.yaml) to a planned test.

result.summary: Design artefact lib/letflow/design/req168-wasm-memory-isolation.md and test/specs/REQ-168.md written for REQ-168 (WASM-08). Design-only, zero implementation code -- @spec/@type/prose only. Every claim about wasmex v0.15.1's real out-of-bounds memory-access behavior was independently live-verified this session (real MIX_ENV=test mix run scripts, WASMEX_BUILD=true, real installed deps/wasmex), not inferred from docs or the library's own @spec annotations (three of which -- get_byte/3, read_binary/4, write_binary/4 -- were found to be incomplete: each can return {:error, _} despite a declared non-error return type). Key live findings, all reproducible via the (git-ignored, scratch/) probe scripts referenced in the design's section 1: (1) Wasmex.Memory.size/2 returns bytes directly, not pages. (2) wasmex's own NIF already cleanly bounds-checks offset-beyond-size, length-past-end, and even a classic native-word wraparound-shaped pair (offset=2^64-10, length=20) for get_byte/set_byte/read_binary/write_binary -- all return a clean {:error, "out of bounds memory access"} tuple, no crash, up through at least length=2^32-1 (the max value a real WASM32 guest's i32-derived pointer/length could ever produce). (3) CRITICAL, previously-undocumented finding: at a magnitude far beyond any real memory region (no genuine WASM32 guest value could reach it) -- observed threshold between 2^32 (still clean) and 2^40 (aborts) -- wasmex's own Rust-side buffer-allocation path is NOT safe: length=2^63 causes an uncatchable native panic ('capacity overflow') in a spawned NIF thread that leaves the calling process's Wasmex.Utils.native_request/1 blocked forever in a timeout-less `receive` (confirmed hung even after a 15s bound); length=2^40 causes a real Rust allocator abort that SIGABRTs the entire OS process (confirmed live: shell exit code 134, 'Aborted (core dumped)') -- under decision 0014's chosen runtime this IS the BEAM node, reproducing WASM-08's literal 'host crash' failure mode for real, not hypothetically. (4) Two independent Wasmex instances of the identical module bytes have genuinely isolated linear memory (write in one never observable via the other), confirmed live. The design (Letflow.Engine.Wasm.MemoryGuard, new module per this project's one-module-per-orthogonal-concern precedent, no new Task.Supervisor needed) closes the extreme-magnitude hazard by performing the entire bounds decision in Elixir's arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic (which cannot wrap at any magnitude, unlike the Rust/fixed-width case the requirement's own framing describes) using the real, freshly-fetched memory size, before any offset/length value is ever handed to wasmex -- so the dangerous magnitudes discovered live are never presented to wasmex at all. Moduledoc requirement cites req165-wasmex-process-boundary.md section 7.2 verbatim for the still-uncovered residual class (a genuine Wasmtime/NIF engine fault unrelated to pointer magnitude). Full traceability table (REQ-168's 6 real acceptance_criteria plus this handoff's own AC1-AC6) to design elements and planned tests included in both files. mix letflow.lint_handoffs run: 0 new violations. No lib/letflow application code, migrations, or existing WASM module (module_registry.ex, capability_gate.ex, plugin_handler.ex) touched.
